title: Bhai Taru Singh, 1745
hook: a young farmer who fed travelers refuses to cut his hair even under torture

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Mani Singh, the scholar. Your line was the scribe stood firm. Today, a farmer, and the end of a hard week of history, with a look back at it. Day two hundred eighty-seven.
screen: `BHAI MANI SINGH — THE SCRIBE STOOD FIRM.`

segments.voice: A knock at the door, late at night. On the step, two strangers, thin, dusty, clearly on the run. Everyone in the village knows that feeding people like this is dangerous. Somebody might be watching. Somebody might talk. You could say you have nothing, and close the door, and nobody would ever blame you. In a small village near Lahore in the 1740s, a young farmer heard knocks like that again and again. He never closed the door. Today: Bhai Taru Singh.
screen: `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR, LATE.` → `STRANGERS ON THE RUN.` → `HE NEVER CLOSED THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Taru Singh was a young farmer who lived with his mother and sister in a village called Poohla, not far from Lahore. These were the years of the price on Sikh heads. The Khalsa bands were hiding in the jungles, and they needed food. Taru Singh grew grain and shared it. Travelers, hunted Sikhs, anyone hungry who came to the door: tradition says his household fed them all, from the little they had. Someone informed on him. In 1745 he was arrested and brought before the governor in Lahore, charged with feeding the rebels. He was offered his life if he gave up his faith and cut his hair. He said his kesh, his uncut hair, was part of his faith, and he would keep it along with his life's breath. The governor's men removed his scalp. Tradition says he bore it with his lips moving in prayer, and that he died soon after. Sikhs remember him in Ardas among those who were scalped rather than give up their kesh. You'll remember kesh from our days on the five Ks: hair kept as it was given. For Taru Singh it wasn't a rule. It was himself. Now look back at this week. The battle inside: the real battle. Banda Singh Bahadur: called to serve. Sirhind: land to the tillers. Banda's end: true to the end. The years in the forests: they survived. Bhai Mani Singh: the scribe stood firm. And Bhai Taru Singh, the farmer who kept feeding strangers, and kept his kesh.
screen: `A FARMER WHO FED THE HUNTED.` · `ARRESTED FOR FEEDING THE REBELS.` · `CUT YOUR HAIR, OR DIE.` · `REMEMBERED IN ARDAS.` · then, large: `HE KEPT HIS KESH.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who could use a meal right now. A friend with a new baby, a coworker on a long shift, a neighbor living alone, someone passing through a hard stretch. Picture them at your door. What could you feed them, a meal, a snack, a coffee, a place at your table? Choose one person and one small way to feed them this week. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Taru Singh. The young farmer who fed hunted Sikhs and travelers, and in 1745 refused to cut his hair to save his life.
Your line: he kept his kesh. Today, feed one person who could use it, even with something small. Day two hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Taru Singh in Ardas among those who gave their scalps rather than their kesh; a gurdwara, Shaheed Ganj Bhai Taru Singh, marks the place in Lahore, and his story is often told to children to explain why Sikhs keep their hair.
